title: İmamoğlu Sentenced to Jail and Political Ban as Armenia-Turkey Border Nears Reopening
subhead: A court hands jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu a two-year prison term and a political ban that could force a new Istanbul mayoral election, while Turkish and Armenian officials say the long-closed border is almost ready to open. Ankara also edges toward first electricity at Akkuyu, its first nuclear plant.

sections.heading: İmamoğlu Gets Jail Term and Political Ban in Insult Retrial
sections.body: Hürriyet Daily News reports that jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu was sentenced on Sept. 11 to 2 years and 1 month in prison and handed a political ban in a retrial over alleged insults against former Tuzla Mayor Şadi Yazıcı. İmamoğlu, already jailed pending trial on corruption allegations involving Istanbul Municipality, had been acquitted twice in the same case three years ago before an appeals court overturned those rulings on procedural grounds. If the ban is not overturned on appeal, it becomes final and triggers a new election among Istanbul Municipality council members to choose the city's mayor — a politically charged prospect in Turkey's largest city, which İmamoğlu won in 2019.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the sharpest legal blow yet to Turkey's most prominent opposition figure, layering a political ban on top of existing corruption proceedings. It deepens the pressure on the CHP and fuels opposition realignment debates just as speculation swirls around İmamoğlu's presidential ambitions.

sections.heading: Armenia-Turkey Border 'Almost Ready to Open,' Both Sides Signal Readiness
sections.body: Turkish special envoy Serdar Kılıç told the Yerevan Dialogue 2026 Forum that the Turkey-Armenia border is 'almost at the point of being ready to open,' while Armenian lawmaker Sargis Khandanyan, chair of the parliamentary external relations committee, said both sides are ready for full normalization, per bianet reporting. The momentum extends beyond the border: eurasianet.org reports Armenia and Turkey are exploring stronger energy connectivity, with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan meeting on the sidelines of an IAEA-sponsored gathering. But the pace is drawing friction — 1news.az (Sept. 7) warns the West is rushing an economic thaw 'bypassing' the Armenia-Azerbaijan track, and eurasiareview.com (Sept. 5) notes Turkey denied reports that French President Emmanuel Macron requested border-crossing permission during a visit to Yerevan.
sections.whyItMatters: After three decades of a closed border, Ankara and Yerevan appear closer than ever to a breakthrough. But opening the border touches the Armenia-Azerbaijan dynamic and Azerbaijan's sensitivities, so the economic track is advancing faster than formal diplomatic recognition — a politically loaded sequencing.

sections.heading: Akkuyu Nears First Electricity as Fuel-Loading Window Opens
sections.body: The first unit of Turkey's Akkuyu nuclear plant, built by Russia's Rosatom, is moving toward start-up. World Nuclear News reports dummy fuel was successfully loaded in Unit 1, and Azernews cites President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan saying 'we have entered the completion phase at Akkuyu.' Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar told state-run Anadolu Agency the first reactor is undergoing intensive testing and will 'go online soon.' Azernews notes that if actual fuel loading happens at the end of September or early October, first electricity could come in the final days of 2026 — but delays could push it into 2027, and full ramp-up is a separate, longer phase.
sections.whyItMatters: Akkuyu is Turkey's first nuclear plant and central to its energy-security ambitions amid high oil prices and the Hormuz closure. Its Russian ownership complicates the picture — the project deepens Ankara-Moscow energy ties even as Turkey balances Western partners — and any start of the schedule matters for Turkey's power mix and import bill.

sections.heading: Quake-Zone Court Frees Column-Cutters Despite 35 Deaths
sections.body: Hürriyet Daily News reports the Kahramanmaraş 4th Court for Serious Crimes, after a 15-hour hearing on Sept. 12, convicted two bakery operators — Sami Kervancıoğlu and Mustafa Pekel — of causing multiple deaths and injuries with conscious negligence over the 2023 earthquake collapse of the Ezgi Apartment, which killed 35 people. Prosecutors had sought 876 years and six months on homicide charges, but the panel instead imposed eight-year sentences and released the pair under judicial control. A building technical supervisor got six years and eight months, while several municipal zoning and construction officials received shorter terms; relatives of victims protested the rulings.
sections.whyItMatters: The case tests Turkey's post-2023 earthquake accountability. Lighter-than-requested sentences and releases in a symbolically charged collapse underscore how uneven the judicial reckoning over construction negligence has been, even as prosecutions continue.

sections.heading: Economy: September Data-Heavy as August Inflation Runs at 31.5%
sections.body: Daily Sabah flags that September is packed with key Turkish economic data alongside a 'new road map,' after Turkish Statistical Institute data (per RTE) showed annual inflation at 31.5% in August, with monthly consumer prices up 1.84%. The new Medium-Term Programme released earlier in September cut the 2026 GDP growth target to 3.3% from a previously stated 3.8%, per BloombergHT via MSN, and the central bank held its policy rate at 37% on Sept. 10. The mix suggests a growth-sacrificing disinflation path now being tested by energy costs, with oil well above the assumptions baked into the plan.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is in a delicate phase: inflation is coming down steadily but remains above 30%, and the government is revising growth targets downward while oil and the Hormuz situation threaten the external balance. The September data run and fiscal roadmap will indicate whether the central bank can stick to its rate-hold without the lira or prices slipping.

sections.heading: Erdoğan-Yavaş Meeting: AKP Spox Calls It 'Only Natural'
sections.body: After President Erdoğan's meeting with Ankara Mayor Mansur Yavaş (covered in the Sept. 11 brief), AKP spokesman Ömer Çelik called the talks 'only natural,' saying they focused solely on capital municipal projects, per Hürriyet Daily News. The meeting nonetheless continues to fuel speculation over Yavaş's political trajectory amid deep divisions in the opposition camp, which has also seen the deposed CHP leadership orbit and talk of a breakaway party.
sections.whyItMatters: No new substance, but the meeting sits at the intersection of two live storylines: Erdoğan's outreach to a popular opposition-held mayoralty and the CHP's internal fragmentation. How Yavaş navigates it shapes the opposition landscape ahead of any election cycle.

bottomLine: On Sept. 13, Turkey's biggest story is domestic and legal: jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu was handed a two-year prison term and a political ban that could force a new Istanbul mayoral election, sharpening pressure on the opposition. In parallel, Ankara is moving on three strategic fronts — a border with Armenia that officials say is almost ready to open, first electricity at the Russian-built Akkuyu nuclear plant that could come by year-end, and a revised economic road map that cuts growth targets while disinflation holds around 31%. The through-line is a government consolidating control at home from the courts outward while expanding its regional and energy footprint, all under the shadow of high oil prices and the Hormuz closure.
sources: Hürriyet Daily News, bianet, eurasianet.org, 1news.az, eurasiareview.com, World Nuclear News, Azernews, Anadolu Agency, Daily Sabah, RTE, BloombergHT via MSN
